facts.label: Proposition 13 base property tax rate
facts.instrument: Cal. Const. art. XIII A § 1; Prop. 13 (1978)
facts.quote: Proposition 13 … limited the property tax rate to 1 percent plus the rate necessary to fund local voter-approved bonded indebtedness
facts.note: The 1% is the statewide base. Actual bills are 1% plus voter-approved debt and fixed charges, which is why the effective rate in both counties is higher than 1.0%.

facts.quote: Effective February 16, 2021

facts.label: Prop 19 transferee must occupy within one year and file homeowners'/disabled-veterans' exemption within one year
facts.quote: The transfer is required to be of a principal residence of the transferor, and become the principal residence of the transferee within one year of the transfer. … The transferee shall file for the homeowners' or disabled veterans' exemption within a year of the transfer
facts.note: § 63.2 was amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 539 (SB 293), effective January 1, 2026 — so this is the current text.

facts.label: Prop 19 exclusion is removed when the heir stops being eligible for the homeowners' exemption
facts.quote: the exclusion shall be removed on the date an eligible transferee … is no longer eligible for either the homeowners' or disabled veterans' exemption
facts.note: THIS IS THE BIGGEST TRAP IN THE WHOLE DECISION. The Prop 19 benefit is conditional on continued owner-occupancy. Move out and rent the house, and the low base year value is replaced by a new base year value as of the lien date after the exclusion drops. The 'rent it out and keep the Prop 13 basis' plan does not exist.

facts.label: Prop 19 value cap formula
facts.quote: If the fair market value … is equal to or more than the sum of the taxable value described in paragraph (1) plus one million dollars ($1,000,000), an amount equal to the fair market value … minus the sum of the taxable value … and one million dollars ($1,000,000).

facts.label: Inflation-adjusted $1M allowance, transfers Feb 16 2025 – Feb 15 2027
facts.quote: Accordingly, the $1 million amount is adjusted to $1,044,586. … for transfers that occur February 16, 2025 through February 15, 2027, the value cap will be the sum of the property's factored base year value plus $1,044,586.
facts.note: Biennial adjustment. Re-read 2026-11-26 in BOE Letter To Assessors 2025/009: $1,044,586 applies to transfers from February 16, 2025 through February 15, 2027. The next adjustment is February 2027 and is not yet published. Any projection into 2040-2050 must therefore be a range, not a constant. See CA-PROP19-ALLOWANCE-FUTURE.

facts.label: Published allowance history
Prop 19 allowance for a 2040-2050 transfer
facts.flag: NOT PUBLISHED. BOE adjusts every two years by the FHFA California House Price Index. The 2040-2050 value cannot be known. The model therefore uses three explicit scenarios instead of a single number: (a) allowance grows only with the CPI 2% cap, (b) allowance grows 3%/yr, (c) allowance grows 4.5%/yr. facts.label: Deadline to file the Prop 19 exclusion claim
facts.value: within 3 years of the transfer, or before transfer to a third party, or before the heir stops occupying — whichever is earliest
facts.quote: Within three years after the date of the purchase or transfer of real property for which the claim is filed, or prior to the transfer of the real property to a third party, or an eligible transferee no longer occupies the residence, whichever is earlier.
facts.note: Distinct from the 1-year occupancy and 1-year exemption-filing clocks, which are shorter and binding. Filing the claim late but within 3 years is allowed, but the occupancy clock is not forgiving.

facts.label: San Francisco documentary transfer tax schedule
facts.authority: San Francisco Office of the Assessor-Recorder
facts.instrument: S.F. Business & Tax Regulations Code art. 12-C
facts.quote: If entire value or consideration is $1,000,000 or more but less than $5,000,000, your tax rate is $3.75 for each $500 or portion thereof.
facts.note: The tier rate applies to the ENTIRE consideration, not marginally. A $4,999,999 sale is 0.75%; a $5,000,000 sale is 2.25% of the whole price. That is a $75,000 cliff at the $5M line. Because the household's SF property is estimated at $1.8M, it sits in the 0.75% tier — but only ~$20k of appreciation away from a reset in a future sale is not a concern here; the cliff matters only if the property is ever valued near $5M.

terms.senior_exemption: Single-family parcel owned and occupied as principal residence by someone 65+ before July 1 of the fiscal year is EXEMPT
terms.rent_pass_through: Owners of rent-controlled units may pass through up to 50% of the tax, capped at $65 per unit, if base rent set before June 1, 2027

facts.note: Apply this to Property B (the SF 3-unit building). A 3-unit building is a multifamily residential parcel: base $249 for the first 5,000 sq ft plus $0.195/sq ft over 5,000, capped at $50,000. For a typical Property B's neighbourhood 3-unit of roughly 3,500-4,500 sq ft, the tax is $249/yr. That is negligible — but the rent pass-through of up to $65/unit materially interacts with the rent-controlled tenancies, and the senior exemption may apply if the owner is 65+ and occupying.

facts.label: San Francisco Residential Rent Stabilization and Arbitration Ordinance
facts.value: in force; annual allowable increase set by Rent Board
facts.authority: San Francisco Residential Rent Stabilization and Arbitration Board
facts.flag: I did not fetch the Rent Board's current allowable-increase figure (sfrb.org). The model uses a 2.0%-3.5% range for rent growth on the two regulated units and flags it. THE ALLOWABLE ANNUAL INCREASE IS A HARD CAP, NOT A FORECAST: rents on the two existing tenancies cannot be raised faster than the Board allows, which means the rent path in this analysis is a FLOOR on the downside and capped on the upside. Verify the current and historic allowable increases before relying on the rent projection.
facts.note: Also: the two units are rent-controlled, so the household cannot re-let at market when a tenant vacates only if the tenancy continues; on vacancy the unit can reset to market under Costa-Hawkins (Civ. Code § 1954.53) — itself flagged as unverified in this session.

facts.label: Behavioral Health Services Tax (formerly Mental Health Services Tax): 1% on taxable income over $1,000,000
facts.quote: Line 62 – Behavioral Health Services Tax. If your taxable income is more than $1,000,000, compute the Behavioral Health Services Tax using whole dollars only: 1. Taxable income from Form 540, line 19. 2. Less: $(1,000,000) 3. Subtotal 4. Tax rate – 1%: .01 5. Behavioral Health Services Tax – Multiply line 3 by line 4.
facts.note: Read 2026-11-26 in the official 2025 Form 540 booklet (line 62). The booklet states a fixed $1,000,000 amount for every filing status. Whether the figure is indexed in later years is not stated in the 2025 booklet, so the 2026 treatment is unverified until the 2026 booklet is published.

facts.label: California top marginal income tax rate
facts.instrument: 2025 California Tax Rate Schedules (Schedules X, Y, Z); Form 540 line 31
facts.note: Read 2026-11-26. Combined top marginal with the 1% Behavioral Health Services Tax is 13.3%: from $1,000,000 for single filers, from $1,010,417 for heads of household, and from $1,485,906 for joint filers. Between $1,000,000 and those thresholds the marginal rate is 12.3%. Statutory thresholds are quoted exactly. The 2025 schedule is the latest published; the 2026 schedule is not yet out.
facts.quote: Schedule X (single or MFS): 12.30% of the amount over $742,953. Schedule Y (MFJ/RDP or QSS): 12.30% over $1,485,906. Schedule Z (head of household): 12.30% over $1,010,417.

facts.label: Property A factored base year value, 2026
facts.flag: Derived from the household's 13-year tax/assessment series, then rounded to a $10,000 band to avoid publishing a parcel-unique figure. The series shows a starting point consistent with a late-1990s/2000 base year plus 2%/yr growth, and an effective tax rate of roughly 1.2%-1.4% of assessed value (above the 1% Prop 13 base, consistent with voter-approved debt and fixed charges). Both the base year value and the effective rate should be read off an actual tax bill.

facts.label: San Francisco property factored base year value, 2025
facts.flag: IRREGULARITY. The household's SF tax bill is roughly $2,400 against an assessed value of roughly $114,000. That is an effective rate near 2.1%, which is roughly DOUBLE the ~1.0%-1.3% seen in Santa Clara County and far above the 1% Prop 13 base plus typical debt. A rate that high against a base-year value that low is unusual. Two explanations fit and they have opposite consequences: (a) the assessed-value column and the tax column are from different years or different parcels, or (b) there are large fixed charges / assessments / bonded debt on this parcel, or (c) the property carries a Mello-Roos or special assessment. MUST be checked against the actual tax bill before any model output is relied upon. Flagged prominently.
facts.note: Note the tax declined 5.9% in 2021 while assessed value rose 1% — inconsistent with a simple 1%+debt formula. Another sign the two columns may not be directly comparable.

facts.label: San Francisco estimated market value, November 2026
facts.flag: HOUSEHOLD ESTIMATE. This is a 3-unit building in Property B's neighbourhood; a 3-unit is valued on gross rent multiplier and comparable 3-unit sales, not on the single-family per-square-foot metric. Obtain a broker opinion of value for a 3-unit specifically.

facts.label: San Francisco 2-of-3 units gross rent
facts.flag: Household figure, unverified. $85,800/yr gross on a $1.8M building is a 4.77% gross yield — plausible for a long-held Property B's neighbourhood 3-unit with below-market tenancies. The third unit is vacant/unrented, which is either a big opportunity (reset to market) or a warning (unrentable as configured). MUST be resolved: is the third unit legal, habitable, and rentable? That single question moves Property B's value by several hundred thousand dollars.
facts.note: Two units rented, one not. If the owner occupies the third unit, Property B is also a principal residence — which changes the § 121 analysis, the Prop 19 analysis if it is ever inherited onward, and the rent-control treatment (owner-occupancy of one unit in a 3-unit building is permitted under SF law; a 3-unit is not covered by the SF condo-conversion lottery in the same way as larger buildings — flagged unverified).

facts.label: Property A utilities: water $100-$150/mo; solar makes electricity ~$0, net credit $10-$20/mo
facts.flag: Household figures. The solar net-credit is a strong assumption: it depends on NEM tariff version, true-up, and whether a future owner inherits the interconnection agreement. NEM 3.0 (net billing) substantially reduces export credit value for systems that are not grandfathered. Whether THIS system is grandfathered should be checked with the utility before the $10-$20 credit is modelled as durable for 30 years. Modelled as a range that decays to $0 net under the adverse case.

facts.label: San Francisco utilities: water $330-$400/mo (3 units); electricity $30-$70/mo
facts.flag: Household figures. Whether these are landlord-paid or tenant-paid is decisive and not stated. If the landlord pays water for all three units and electricity for common areas, that is a real ~$4,800/yr expense; if tenants pay, it is zero. Modelled both ways.

facts.label: Property A homeowners insurance, annual
facts.authority: Household; no official source exists for a single parcel
facts.flag: The household guessed ~$1,500. That is almost certainly too low for a $3.1M replacement-cost dwelling in Santa Clara County in the current admitted/non-admitted market. There is no official published rate for a specific parcel. Modelled as a $1,500-$4,500/yr range with the midpoint used for the headline, and flagged. ACTION: get three real quotes. California FAIR Plan exposure and wildfire/brush zone status should be checked; foothill parcels in the county are often in a higher fire severity zone than flatland parcels; Property A's own zone is not yet checked.

facts.label: Property A maintenance and capital reserve, annual
facts.unit: percent of market value per year
facts.authority: Household ('regular maintenance and repair costs, not as much as the San Francisco house')
facts.flag: No official source. The 0.5%-1.25% band is a common planning heuristic, not a measured figure, and it is published here as a heuristic. A 50-year-old single-family house in Santa Clara County will have lumpy capital events (roof, sewer lateral, foundation, HVAC, windows) that a percentage-of-value model smooths away. ACTION: build the five-year maintenance and capital plan the household asked for, using actual contractor quotes.

facts.label: San Francisco maintenance and capital reserve, annual
facts.unit: percent of market value per year
facts.authority: Household ('not as much as...' reversed: household says SF needs MORE regular maintenance)
facts.flag: No official source. A 3-unit pre-war Property B's neighbourhood building carries more maintenance per dollar than a single-family house: three kitchens, three baths, shared systems, seismic, and rent-controlled tenants whose repair requests cannot be declined. Banded higher than Property A for that reason.
